title: Atomic Structure: From Dalton to Quantum Numbers

questions.question: Who discovered the neutron, and in which year?
questions.rationale: Chadwick detected the neutral particle in 1932. Thomson found the electron (1897), Rutherford proposed the nucleus (1911), and Goldstein observed canal rays (1886).

questions.question: In Rutherford's gold foil experiment, most α-particles passed straight through the foil. This showed that:
options: electrons carry most of the mass
the atom is mostly empty space
questions.rationale: Straight passage meant the atom's body holds almost no matter; the rare large deflections came from a concentrated positive charge.

questions.question: About 1 in 20,000 α-particles bounced almost straight back because:
options: a tiny, dense, positive nucleus repelled and turned them
the gold foil was too thick
questions.rationale: Only a concentrated positive charge could reverse a fast, heavy α-particle — the key evidence for the nuclear model.

questions.question: The 'plum pudding' model of the atom was proposed by:
questions.rationale: J. J. Thomson imagined electrons embedded in a sphere of positive charge, like plums in a pudding.

questions.question: According to the Pauli exclusion principle, a single orbital can hold:
questions.rationale: No two electrons in an atom share all four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most two electrons, with spins opposed.

questions.question: Hund's rule states that electrons entering a set of equal-energy orbitals:
options: occupy orbitals singly with parallel spins before any pairing
questions.rationale: Degenerate orbitals each gain one electron, spins parallel, before pairing begins.

questions.question: The electron configuration of potassium (Z = 19) is:
questions.rationale: By the Aufbau order the 4s subshell fills before 3d, so potassium is [Ar] 4s¹ with one valence electron.

questions.question: Tritium (³H) contains how many neutrons?
questions.rationale: Tritium has 1 proton and mass number 3, so it contains 3 − 1 = 2 neutrons; protium has none and deuterium has one.

questions.question: ⁴⁰Ar and ⁴⁰Ca are examples of:
questions.rationale: Isobars share a mass number (here 40) but differ in proton count; isotopes instead share the proton count.

questions.question: Bohr's model won lasting fame because it explained:
questions.rationale: Fixed orbits allow only definite energy jumps with ΔE = hν, matching hydrogen's sharp emission lines — though the model fails for multi-electron atoms.
